title.en: Unit 4 · Statistical Inference: Proportions, Means & Slopes

body.en: Statistical inference draws conclusions about unknown population parameters from sample data. The two primary pillars are confidence intervals (estimating parameters) and significance tests (assessing evidence regarding claims).

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Confidence Intervals & Margin of Error

body.en: Construct confidence intervals using the standard anatomy \(\text{statistic} \pm (\text{critical value})(\text{standard error})\), and master formal contextual interpretations.

\[ \text{Confidence Interval} = \text{Point Estimate} \pm \text{Margin of Error} = \text{Statistic} \pm (\text{Critical Value}) \times (\text{Standard Error}). \]

Formal Interpretation of Confidence Interval: 'We are C% confident that the interval from [lower] to [upper] captures the true [population parameter in context].'

Formal Interpretation of Confidence Level: 'If we were to take many random samples of the same size from this population and construct a C% confidence interval from each sample, about C% of the intervals would capture the true [population parameter in context].'

title.en: ⊙ Explorer · Margin of error vs. sample size

ariaLabel.en: A confidence interval around x-bar shrinking as sample size n increases

caption.en: The sample statistics and the resulting confidence interval

note.en: Slide \(n\) to see the margin of error shrink in proportion to \(1/\sqrt{n}\). To halve the margin of error, you need four times the sample size.

body.en:
A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of registered voters who support an education bond is \((0.52, 0.58)\). Interpret this interval in context, and determine whether there is convincing evidence that a majority supports the bond.

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.52 to 0.58 (or 52% to 58%) captures the true proportion of all registered voters who support the bond.

Conclusion: Yes, because the entire 95% confidence interval lies strictly above 0.50 (50%), there is convincing statistical evidence that a majority of registered voters support the bond.

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

A random sample of 100 high school seniors finds that 64 plan to attend a four-year college. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true population proportion \(p\) of seniors attending a four-year college.

solution.en:
Point estimate: \(\hat{p} = \frac{64}{100} = 0.64\). Critical value: \(z^* = 1.96\).

Standard error: \[ \text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.64(0.36)}{100}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.2304}{100}} = 0.048. \]

Margin of error: \[ \text{ME} = 1.96 \times 0.048 = 0.09408 \approx 0.094. \]

Confidence interval: \[ 0.64 \pm 0.094 = \mathbf{(0.546, 0.734)}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Hypothesis Testing Logic, Test Statistics & p-Values

body.en: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses, compute standardized test statistics, calculate p-values, and articulate statistical decisions.

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): A statement of 'no difference' or 'no effect' (parameter = hypothesized value).

Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_a\)): The claim we suspect or are testing for (parameter <, >, or \(\neq\) hypothesized value).

p-value: The probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the observed value, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

Decision Rule:

  • If \(\text{p-value} \le \alpha\): Reject \(H_0\); there is convincing statistical evidence for \(H_a\).
  • If \(\text{p-value} > \alpha\): Fail to reject \(H_0\); there is insufficient statistical evidence for \(H_a\).

A factory claims its candy machines produce bags with an average weight of 50.0 grams. A consumer group tests \(H_0: \mu = 50.0\) vs \(H_a: \mu < 50.0\) using a sample of 25 bags, finding \(\bar{x} = 49.2\text{ g}\) and \(s = 1.5\text{ g}\). Compute the \(t\) test statistic and conclude at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

Compute test statistic: \[ t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{49.2 - 50.0}{1.5 / \sqrt{25}} = \frac{-0.8}{0.3} = -2.67 \quad (df = 24). \]

From the \(t\)-distribution with \(df = 24\), \(P(T < -2.67) \approx 0.0067\).

Because the p-value \(0.0067 < \alpha = 0.05\), we reject \(H_0\). There is convincing evidence that the true mean bag weight is less than 50.0 grams.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

A significance test produces a test statistic of \(z = 2.15\) for a two-sided test \(H_0: p = 0.40\) vs \(H_a: p \neq 0.40\). What is the p-value, and what decision is made at \(\alpha = 0.05\)?

solution.en:
For a standard normal distribution, \(P(Z > 2.15) = 1 - 0.9842 = 0.0158\).

Since the alternative hypothesis is two-sided (\(\neq\)), multiply by 2: \[ \text{p-value} = 2 \times 0.0158 = \mathbf{0.0316}. \]

Because \(\text{p-value} = 0.0316 < \alpha = 0.05\), we reject \(H_0\). There is convincing statistical evidence that the true population proportion differs from 0.40.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Two-Sample Tests, Paired Data, Chi-Square & Regression Slopes

body.en: Select the correct inference procedure among two-sample t-tests, paired t-tests, chi-square tests, and linear regression t-tests for slope, and verify all necessary assumptions.

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Statistical Inference

body.en:
• Two-Sample t-Test vs. Paired t-Test: If two sets of data come from the SAME subjects (before/after) or matched pairs, use a one-sample paired t-test on differences \(d = x_1 - x_2\). If data come from two independent groups, use a two-sample t-test.
  • Chi-Square Goodness of Fit vs Independence: Goodness of fit tests a single categorical variable against a specified distribution. Chi-Square Test of Independence tests for an association between two categorical variables in a two-way contingency table.
  • Slope Hypothesis Test: For linear regression slope \(\beta\), \(H_0: \beta = 0\) tests whether there is a statistically significant linear relationship between \(x\) and \(y\).
  • Condition Verification: State condition, write formula/numbers, check: Random (stated), 10% condition (\(10n \le N\)), and Normality/Large Counts (e.g. \(n_1\hat{p}_1 \ge 10\)).

A computer printout for a linear regression model yields: Predictor: Constant Coef = 12.4, SE = 2.1; Slope Coef = 3.65, SE = 0.73, t = 5.00, p = 0.0001 with \(n = 20\). Test \(H_0: \beta = 0\) vs \(H_a: \beta \neq 0\) at \(\alpha = 0.01\).

The test statistic for the slope is: \[ t = \frac{b - 0}{\text{SE}_b} = \frac{3.65}{0.73} = 5.00 \quad (df = n - 2 = 18). \]

Because the p-value \(0.0001 < 0.01\), we reject \(H_0\). There is convincing statistical evidence of a linear relationship between the explanatory and response variables.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Ten athletes participate in a vertical jump training program. Their jump heights (in inches) before and after the program are recorded. To test whether the program increased jump height, explain why a paired t-test is appropriate rather than a two-sample t-test, state the null and alternative hypotheses, and specify the degrees of freedom.

solution.en:
Why Paired: The observations are paired on the same subjects (before and after measurements on each athlete). The two samples are dependent, not independent.

Hypotheses: Letting \(\mu_d = \mu_{\text{after}} - \mu_{\text{before}}\) be the true mean difference in jump height: \[ H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_a: \mu_d > 0. \]

Degrees of Freedom: Since this is a one-sample test on differences: \[ df = n - 1 = 10 - 1 = \mathbf{9}. \]
